“I’ve made every component before,” Jesse tells his cohost Shilpa Uskokovic. “I just haven’t arranged the puzzle pieces in this fashion.”
“We hope that that's what people in Bake Club take away,” Shilpa adds. “That by having these building blocks, you can make all these things, even if they’re the first time you’re making them.”
Jesse’s version has an American twist (a no-bake cheesecake filling) and a nod to his Polish roots (the plum compote).

text:
For the past six years, senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewyczk has been trying to get a karpatka recipe published. Even though he’d never made one in its entirety before. But he knew BA’s Bake Club was the perfect place to showcase what he calls the drag queen of Polish desserts.

“I’ve made every component before,” Jesse tells his cohost Shilpa Uskokovic. “I just haven’t arranged the puzzle pieces in this fashion.”

“We hope that that's what people in Bake Club take away,” Shilpa adds. “That by having these building blocks, you can make all these things, even if they’re the first time you’re making them.”

Jesse’s version has an American twist (a no-bake cheesecake filling) and a nod to his Polish roots (the plum compote).

Listeners also weighed in with questions about and photos of their sky-high desserts, and we awarded our Baker of the Month. We also had a visit from a beloved star baker in The Great British Baking Show (a.k.a. Bake-Off for those in the UK). Season nine finalist Ruby Bhogal stopped by the podcast to talk about her new book Around the World in 80 Cakes. And yes, there is a karpatka in it!

Find Ruby Bhogal @rubybhogal and on Substack.

Shilpa Uskokovic: I'm Shilpa Uskokovic.

Jesse Szewczyk: And I'm Jesse Szewczyk.

SU: We're both senior test kitchen editors at Bon Appétit.

JS: And this is BA Bake Club.

SU: Bake Club is Bon Appétit's community of confident and curious bakers.

JS: We're creating the nerdiest and most wholesome corner of the baking internet.

SU: Every month, we publish a recipe on bonappetit.com that introduces a baking concept that we think you should know.

JS: Then you'll go bake, and you can send us any questions you have or pictures of your finished creations.

SU: And we get together here on the podcast to talk about the recipe.

JS: The September Bake Club recipe for glazed apple pie fritters is live now on bonappetit.com, and we'll tell you a bit more about those at the end of the episode.

SU: But today, today we're diving into Jesse's Polish roots with his recipe for a Plum Karpatka.

JS: Listen, I've been pitching of Karpatka for years.

SU: You have?

JS: Okay, I'm going to be real. I didn't grow up eating Karpatka. And we'll explain to you what this is. I feel like I'm building suspense here.

SU: Yes.

JS: But it's this Polish cake that I stumbled across several years ago, and I was like, "This is cool."

SU: How do you describe it in your text? I love the phrase that you use.

JS: Oh, and they let me keep it. I called it the drag queen of Polish desserts because it's just big, boisterous, and kind of silly.

SU: Showy.

JS: Yeah.

SU: It's a lovely dessert.

JS: Thank you.

SU: And you gave it a really nice ... In a way, it was almost like a very New York spin with a cheesecake.

JS: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

SU: That's the whole thing. Okay. The photos that our Bake Clubbers have sent in of the Karpatka have been absolutely incredible.

JS: They're big. Yeah.

SU: I feel like there were a lot of skills that came together in this one from past Bake Club bakes.

JS: Yeah. Those of you who have been around for a while, we did a Paris-Brest, which is this big kind of tire of choux that you fill with a sweet filling.

SU: And for those who are listening, it's choux, as in choux pastry.

JS: Choux paste, yes.

SU: Okay. Sorry, Jesse. Didn't mean to cut you off.

JS: Not the gym shoes, a big tire of choux. And that was a traditional way to cook pâte à choux, you can make cream puffs, éclairs. And this is baking choux in a cake pan, which I feel like is a very unique way to bake it. So, it's like building upon that foundation we learned several months back to create something completely different.

SU: I love that you did that, because that's what baking is about. It's like these few things that you have, and then you re-spin it in different directions. Okay. Before we go any further, let's take a moment to get a brief step-by-step tour of this recipe. Okay? And for that, we're going to need our jaunty Bake Club music. Here it is. Okay. Jesse, walk us through this recipe.

JS: Yeah, and buckle up because it's a challenge. Not hard, but it takes some effort. Okay, let's start.

SU: Sure.

JS: So, you're first going to start by making plum compote, and that's very easy. You just cook some plums with sugar and salt. And then when that's nice and thick, you're just going to finish it with some lemon zest juice and some vanilla, and that's your jam. So, make sure you cool that though, because it'd be warm, you need it to be nice and cool and thick.

So, as that's cooling, you're going to make your pâte à choux, which we might be familiar with. So, you're going to bring a stick of butter, cut into little pieces, some sugar, some salt, and water to a simmer. And with simmering, you're going to add some flour, and then cook that into this thick doughy paste, and then take that out, let it cool for a while, and then you're going to whip that in a mixer with some eggs.

Divide that between two cake bands and bake them, and then watch as they dramatically turn into these giant wonky discs. So, cool your discs, and as those are cooling, you can work on your filling. So, this is like a no-bake cheesecake.

So, you're going to start by blooming some gelatin in some cold water, let that sit, then heat up just a tiny bit of cream, pour that over that, so it dissolves the gelatin. And then, to that, you're going to add some cream cheese, some powdered sugar, some vanilla, some salt, and then you're going to beat that all together while adding some more heavy cream to kind of lighten it. And then that's your filling. So, you can assemble everything at this point.

So, those two choux puff discs you have, you keep one in a cake pan, and then you put your filling in, you swirl it with the jam, put the other on top like a sandwich, let it sit overnight, and it sets into this beautiful Karpatka. And that's that.

JS: The drag queen, that's how the drag queen gets her beat on, the full beat.

JS: I'm being called out, and the answer is honestly no.

JS: So, this was a learning experience for us all.

SU: Yes.

JS: Yeah, and it was really fun.

JS: Well, I've made every component.

SU: Exactly.

SU: Exactly.

JS: Yes.

JS: Shilpa, that's beautiful.

SU: Thank you. Okay. What occasion do people ... Well, it's a cake. You can eat it at any time. But traditionally, I wonder when a Karpatka is usually served and eaten.

JS: I think traditionally in Polish culture, it's for holidays, like Easter, Christmas, and I guess this was my summer version. The flirty summer version of a Karpatka.
